title: Resurrecting the Real Monroe Doctrine
gist: University of Toronto political scientist Arturo Chang argues that James Monroe's Dec. 2, 1823 address was a hemispheric solidarity and mutual-defense doctrine, not a claim of U.S. primacy, and that every subsequent corollary — Roosevelt 1904, Kennedy in the Cuban missile crisis, Reagan in Central America, and Trump's own corollary issued last December — has progressively inverted it. He ties this to the live 2026 use of the doctrine to oppose Chinese investment in Latin America and justify intervention in Venezuela and Iran.

themes.theme: Trump's Monroe corollary as intervention license

insights.claim: Trump issued his own corollary to the Monroe Doctrine last December, whose statement declares that the American people — not foreign nations nor globalist institutions — will always control their own destiny in the hemisphere.
insights.speaker: Arturo Chang
insights.so_what: A formal presidential corollary is a standing doctrinal justification for hemispheric intervention; it raises the baseline probability of U.S. action against Latin American governments and of restrictions on non-U.S. investment there.
insights.quote: the American people—not foreign nations nor globalist institutions—will always control their own destiny in our hemisphere.
insights.locator: Trump, of course, now turns to the doctrine

insights.claim: Trump and members of the Republican establishment have leveraged the Monroe Doctrine's legacy to argue against Chinese investment in Latin America and to justify intervention in countries such as Iran and Venezuela.
insights.speaker: Arturo Chang
insights.so_what: Chinese-financed infrastructure, ports and mining in Latin America now sits inside a declared U.S. doctrinal exclusion zone — a concrete political risk for Belt-and-Road-linked assets in the region.

insights.claim: The Trump White House reads the Monroe Doctrine as a declaration that Washington should lead the hemisphere and guard it against communism, fascism, and foreign infringement, explicitly linking America First to the 1823 principle in its 250th anniversary programming.
insights.speaker: Arturo Chang
insights.so_what: The administration is building an official historical narrative that legitimizes hemispheric enforcement, so expect doctrine-framed policy actions rather than ad hoc ones.
insights.quote: against communism, fascism, and foreign infringement

insights.claim: The word homeland in Trump's corollary statement quickly expands into a claim of U.S. leadership over the entire hemisphere that ignores the bonds between American states.
insights.speaker: Arturo Chang
insights.so_what: Watch for homeland-defense language being used to extend jurisdiction well beyond U.S. borders — a rhetorical tell that precedes extraterritorial action.
insights.quote: Monroe declared before the Nation a simple truth that has echoed throughout the ages: The United States will never waver in defense of our homeland, our interests, or the well-being of citizens.

themes.theme: The original 1823 doctrine was solidarity, not supremacy

insights.claim: The Monroe Doctrine originates in James Monroe's seventh annual message to Congress on Dec. 2, 1823, and its opening asserted that the American continents were no longer subjects for future European colonization while simultaneously recognizing the independent condition of the newly sovereign American states.
insights.speaker: Arturo Chang
insights.so_what: The doctrine's text does not support U.S. primacy claims, giving Latin American governments a legitimate textual basis to contest Washington's framing.
insights.locator: What is now referred to as the Monroe Doctrine

insights.claim: Monroe's 1823 address centered mutual defense and shared destinies among American brethren, warning that European intervention anywhere in the continent would endanger U.S. peace and happiness, rather than asserting national superiority.
insights.speaker: Arturo Chang
insights.so_what: The revisionist historical reading undercuts the doctrinal cover for unilateral intervention, an argument regional governments can be expected to deploy diplomatically.

insights.claim: Mexico's 1814 constitution called for universal citizenship for all Americans born in the hemisphere, and Peru's 1821 play The Patriots of Lima on the Happy Night celebrated the emancipation of all Americans rather than only national citizenries.
insights.speaker: Arturo Chang
insights.so_what: Hemispheric identity has deep documentary roots that Latin American leaders can mobilize as a counter-narrative to America First framing.

insights.claim: American thinkers including Alexander Hamilton, Jose Maria Morelos and Simon Bolivar broke with Montesquieu and Rousseau by arguing that large, diverse republics were not only possible in the Americas but potentially more resilient than small ones.
insights.speaker: Arturo Chang
insights.so_what: The scale-resilience argument is a reusable mental model: diversity and size as sources of durability rather than fragility, applicable to any large federated system.

insights.claim: Theodore Roosevelt used the Monroe Doctrine in 1904 to justify U.S. intervention in Central American, Caribbean and South American countries, an interpretation now known as the Roosevelt Corollary.
insights.speaker: Arturo Chang
insights.so_what: The corollary mechanism has a 120-year track record of converting a defensive principle into an interventionist one — precedent for how Trump's version will be operationalized.

insights.claim: John F. Kennedy invoked the Monroe Doctrine during the Cuban missile crisis to justify hemispheric security frameworks under the Rio Pact and the Organization of American States, and Ronald Reagan expanded those interpretations to justify intervention in Nicaragua and El Salvador on claims of Soviet influence.
insights.speaker: Arturo Chang
insights.so_what: External-power-influence claims are the recurring trigger for U.S. hemispheric action; the Chinese-investment framing is the modern equivalent of the Soviet-influence framing.

insights.claim: Each iteration of the Monroe Doctrine throughout U.S. history has moved further away from the original address's principles and vision, making the received imperial reading a two-century accumulation of overwriting rather than an accurate account of 1823.
insights.speaker: Arturo Chang
insights.so_what: Doctrinal drift is cumulative and one-directional, so the next corollary should be expected to expand rather than constrain the scope of claimed U.S. authority.
insights.quote: Each iteration throughout U.S. history has moved further and further away from the original address’s principles and vision.

themes.theme: The reliability question in U.S.-Latin American ties

insights.claim: At the 1826 Panama Congress, Gran Colombian vice president Francisco de Paula Santander invited U.S. representatives partly on the basis of Monroe's 1823 principles, while Simon Bolivar opposed their inclusion out of skepticism that the United States could be a reliable ally — and no U.S. delegation ultimately attended.
insights.speaker: Arturo Chang
insights.so_what: The reliability doubt is 200 years old and unresolved, which is why Latin American hedging toward China and other partners is structural rather than reactive.

insights.claim: The 19th-century Latin American skepticism about U.S. reliability remains directly relevant today as regional leaders continue to question the dependability of U.S. ties under the Trump administration.
insights.speaker: Arturo Chang
insights.so_what: Expect Latin American governments to keep diversifying trade and security partners regardless of U.S. doctrinal assertions — pressure alone will not reverse Chinese commercial penetration.

themes.theme: Competing American identities at the 250th anniversary

insights.claim: The 250th anniversary of U.S. independence has surfaced two competing definitions of American identity: a state-centered project defined by jurisdictional boundaries and physical separation, versus a hemispheric definition based on shared experiences, cultures and diasporas spanning the entire Western Hemisphere.
insights.speaker: Arturo Chang
insights.so_what: The identity contest is the substrate of U.S. immigration, trade and hemispheric policy fights, and it will shape domestic political alignment through the anniversary year.

insights.claim: Popular culture has become a vehicle for the hemispheric conception of American identity, as when Bad Bunny deployed that framing during the Super Bowl LX halftime show while critiquing U.S. imperial tendencies.
insights.speaker: Arturo Chang
insights.so_what: Mass-audience cultural platforms are now contested political terrain for hemispheric identity, a channel with reach that formal diplomacy lacks.
insights.locator: This framing was famously deployed by Bad Bunny

insights.claim: The White House frames the goal of its 250th anniversary programming as inspiring a renewed love for American history, making historical nostalgia an explicit instrument of the go-it-alone state-centered narrative.
insights.speaker: Arturo Chang
insights.so_what: State-sponsored historical programming is being used as policy infrastructure, so anniversary messaging is a leading indicator of doctrinal direction.
insights.quote: inspire a renewed love for American history
